newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine plans to boost electricity exports.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine plans to boost electricity exports.

text.p: Ukraine, a major electricity exporter in Soviet days, plans to increase exports but first must seek investments for its ageing thermal power production facilities, top energy officials said on Tuesday.

Anatoly Batalov, head of Ukraine's dispatching centre which regulates electricity supplies and controls the country's grid, said the country had been exporting 4.5 billion kilowatt hours of electricity a year since 1995 but planned to boost that to 15-16 billion kilo-watt hours by 2000.
"The plan is 15-16 billion, but serious work must be done for modernisation and establishment of a stable frequency in our grid to enable increased exports," Batalov told Reuters.
Ukraine, when it was part of the former Soviet Union, exported up to 30 billion kilowatt-hours mostly to other Soviet satellites in Eastern and Central Europe.
But between 1991, when Ukraine won independence, and 1995, Kiev only exported tiny amounts of electricity to Bulgaria.
Batalov said foreign consumers of Ukrainian electricity in the last three years had been Hungary, Slovakia and Poland.
In exchange Ukraine has been importing Polish coal for its Burshtynska thermal station in western Ukraine, which works exclusively for export purposes and is separate from Ukraine's electricity grid.
Batalov said electricity made from Polish coal is 40 percent cheaper than from Ukrainian coal brought from the eastern coal-mining Donbass area.

Deputy Energy and Electricity Minister Yuri Ulitich told a news conference earlier that earnings from exports also helped pay energy debts to Russia and reconstruction of the Burshtynska plant, which Batalov said needed $80 million in investments.
Ulitych said some $100 million should be spent stabilising the grid's frequency at 50 mega-hertz from 49.35 to 49.55 mega-hertz now.
"If this work is completed in several years we will export electricity also to the Czech Republic, Romania, Bulgaria, Austria, the Balkans and Turkey," Batalov said.
He said last year that Ukraine had produced 181 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity compared to 300 billion in 1990 -- a year before the Soviet Union fell apart.

Ukraine's 41 thermal power stations, some using old and inefficient equipment, produce 51 percent of the country's electricity while five nuclear plants, including the Chernobyl power station, produce 45 per cent.
The rest comes from six hydrostations, built in the 1930s when Soviet dictator Josef Stalin promoted industrialisation on the flat Dnipro river.
